claims.text: The material is a quaternary equiatomic alloy with an FCC crystal structure.
Plastic deformation under uniaxial tension in quaternary equiatomic FCC alloys is governed by dislocation glide.
Yield strength becomes insensitive to strain rate at high temperatures.
High-temperature strain-rate insensitivity occurs because thermally activated dislocation motion is no longer rate-limiting.
Varying tensile strain rate and temperature will alter dislocation density and mobility within the FCC lattice.
Thermally activated dislocation glide over short-range obstacles dominates yielding at lower temperatures and higher strain rates.
Relevant short-range obstacles may include solute atoms and precipitates.
Athermal glide or phonon drag dominates at high temperatures and low strain rates.
Dominance of athermal glide or phonon drag at high temperatures and low strain rates leads to strain-rate-insensitive yielding.
Yield strength will have a strong positive dependence on strain rate at low temperatures.
Yield strength will transition to a strain-rate-insensitive plateau at high temperatures.
At the predicted high-temperature plateau, the activation energy for dislocation motion is negligible relative to thermal energy.
Standard dislocation theory for FCC metals predicts that rate sensitivity diminishes as temperature increases.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the material remains a pure FCC phase.
A stress-induced FCC-to-HCP or FCC-to-BCC transformation could introduce a different rate-sensitive deformation mechanism.
Deformation twinning could introduce a different rate-sensitive deformation mechanism.
Emergence and growth of a new phase concurrent with yielding and strain-rate-insensitive strength would falsify the claim that dislocation glide is the primary mechanism.
